01 · How I can help

What business needs now

I can connect strategy, operations, technology and the real work of people. Four current top-level challenges from my experience, and a fifth, new one: AI that really improves efficiency.

  1. Bringing operations and the commercial side together in tools that drive financial results

    Give operational teams the tools they need in their daily work to see their contribution and manage results. At Silpo, store managers received their store’s P&L, and the commercial division saw the profitability of every product category in every store after all costs.

    The store P&L was available by the 5th of the following month and showed only the costs a manager can influence. For categories, we took into account shelf space, the area of production zones, equipment energy use, driver-based cost allocation, and price promotions and other promotional activities, to see real profitability. Production areas turned out to be especially sensitive, for example: they have higher utility costs and more expensive skilled staff.

  2. A balanced scorecard (BSC) that worked in practice

    At Silpo, I introduced management by objectives to balance the metrics of different functions against each other: goals cascaded from the C-level down to every store, with plan vs. actual in operational dashboards. Every week and month, each store received an overall score: customers, staff, processes, finance, productivity.

    Data was rolled up by store group, region and the whole chain, with trends by month, quarter and year. Metrics had different weights, and finance was only part of the score. Over-achievement on many metrics was capped, so as not to reward what the team does not control: for example, higher revenue because a carnival that nobody had planned for passed nearby.

  3. Managing workforce productivity: from the annual budget to yesterday’s plan vs. actual

    At Silpo, I ran a project to set labour standards for store processes based on revenue. On that basis, I built the annual budget planning system and introduced operational tools to control shift planning and target achievement by day and week. This made it possible to adjust the workload in time to meet monthly payroll targets. The result: a controlled impact on EBITDA.

    Staffing needs (FTE) were calculated from planned revenue, processes and the target service level. Then came monthly plans, HR hiring plans that allowed for seasonality and staff turnover, and weekly shift schedules. Actuals were checked against receipts, sales and staff clock-in and clock-out records.

  4. Extensive experience of systemic change: acquisitions, restructurings and building a PMO

    At Silpo, I built and led the project management office (PMO). I know how to set up a PMO as the centre of change management in a company. Management can then see what works, what blocks results and where a decision is needed. Every change is locked into processes and into control and monitoring systems, and cascaded through metrics and goals.

    While I worked at Silpo, the chain grew from about 120 to 300 stores. I ran large acquisition and restructuring projects, merged more than 20 legal entities into one and designed an organisational structure for managing change in the stores. I delivered a systemic change across the whole chain: new processes and risk-based cycle counting (calculating what to count and when in partial counts during the year) led to an annual full stocktake instead of a monthly one, and automation on a mobile platform helped lock in the changes and repeat this and dozens of other processes over time.

  5. The new challenge: systematic use of AI that genuinely improves efficiency, with a controlled payback

    Everything is changing very fast now, and there is no time to wait until the old processes are put in order. I propose not just adding AI to existing processes, even ones revised “for AI”, but rebuilding how the company works together with people who already know how to work with AI and use that knowledge to shape requirements and the vision. It is important to build “Digital Management”: a single, transparent system for running the company and making decisions. Research by leading analysts supports this: the gains appear when work is rebuilt with AI from the start.

    1. Engage and train people: give them a personal AI assistant so they take the first steps themselves, create their own solutions and feel the power of the exoskeleton.
    2. Let the people who run the processes redesign them, with outside consultants where needed.
    3. Build a company-wide system for knowledge, risk assessment and company management. I see three ways to use AI: faster IT development, broader analytics, and AI in products and processes that takes over routine work while decisions stay with people.
02 · First steps

How I see the first 100 days

AI can bring quick results, but how far they go depends on which data the company’s security rules allow AI to work with. So I start by assessing these constraints. Using AI effectively under strict security requirements is often a task of its own.

  1. Goals and directionUnderstand where the company is going: its goals, priorities and the direction of change.
  2. Pain points and quick winsFind the most pressing problems and the areas that can deliver quick, tangible results, so the start pays for itself right away.
  3. Team, plan, deliveryForm the team, set goals, draw up plans, then coordinate and implement. With AI, each step goes much faster than usual.
  4. Scaling AIHow AI is scaled depends on the company’s goals and the role it gives to AI. It can mean building new solutions, helping each employee in their daily work, or a company-wide system that connects people’s knowledge and work.

PMO Hub is a toolkit that helps managers organise and coordinate projects, from a department up to a whole project office. I already run my own work with it. PMO Hub started as a tool for managing the development of DPA, and later both of my car-audio projects were built with it.

Public · 2 repositories

Autosound: Tuning Skill and TCC

Skill on GitHub ↗ TCC on GitHub ↗

One project in two parts for tuning car audio built around a sound processor. I gathered the approaches, documentation, instructions, libraries and experience (mine and friends’), and with AI’s help built the skill on that base: it makes the overall process deterministic while keeping AI flexible at every step. The skill follows a seven-phase algorithm, from intake to final listening, and works through many interacting factors at once: the car's acoustics, every speaker, crossovers, time delays, phase and equalisation. Real measurements and maths lead it to the best settings. The skill works in Claude, Codex and Antigravity.

TCC is a full desktop application built on top of the skill: multilingual, for macOS and Windows, with live measurements, the predicted result, the tuning plan and an AI chat panel. It works together with the skill and can use different AI models, directly or through the OMP tool.

In both, Claude calculates and proposes settings, a model from another vendor checks, critiques and corrects them, and the person listens and decides. Nothing changes the processor by itself.

7phases in one fixed tuning process
14major and minor releases of the skill since June 2026
4,300+automated tests in TCC
4languages; macOS and Windows

Results in 2026: my own car won five awards at EMMA and AYA championships, including two first places in qualifying rounds and third at the German EMMA Final. One user’s car took first place at the AYA Finale.

Oleksandr brings operations, commerce, finance and IT into one system that can be managed through metrics. He builds not a one-off result but a mechanism: standards, budget, plan vs. actual, targets, and he locks changes into processes and controls. He makes sure metrics are fair: only the costs a manager can influence, and no rewards for luck. He understands technology from the inside, from electronics to code. When working together, he insists on facts: he checks every phrase and cuts out hype.
